title: WHY AFRICAN PENGUINS KEEP COMBING THEIR FEATHERS
caption: African penguins have a reason for all that grooming. 🐧 #AfricanPenguin #OceanLife #Wildlife #WildVox

narration_timeline.text: Why do African penguins spend so much time grooming with their bills?
narration_timeline.scene: Real two African penguins visibly grooming in Wuppertal Zoo, Germany. Source 06 original 0–4.8s selected after 2026-10-28 independent 1.9/8.1/13.7s preview; confirm visible bill-to-feather contact in final rendered opening, with captive setting disclosed.

narration_timeline.text: Along southern Africa's coast, these birds move between ocean feeding trips and land.
narration_timeline.scene: Authentic South African coastal colony: independent Angelarene88 source starts near 20s showing visibly close African penguins at Betty's Bay, then distinct real penguins walking. No claim that ocean feeding is visible.

narration_timeline.text: Back ashore, they preen, cleaning and lining up their tightly packed feathers.
narration_timeline.scene: Authentic African penguins combing feathers on rocky shore at Stony Point, illustrating cleaning and feather alignment; the original combing footage moves to the action block rather than the hook.

narration_timeline.text: Their tightly packed feathers help keep cold water away from the skin.
narration_timeline.scene: Close African penguin plumage at the edge of a zoo pool in authentic Guido Konrad slow-motion footage; illustrative captive scene, not South African sea footage or proof of seawater waterproofing.

narration_timeline.text: But they also need safe places on land where they can shelter and breed.
narration_timeline.scene: African penguins near an actual den at Stony Point.

narration_timeline.text: So the constant grooming is more than fussing. It's upkeep for a life split between sea and shore.
narration_timeline.scene: Authentic portrait African penguin walking from shore toward the sea, first seconds of Boulders Beach source, followed by distinct colony footage.
